pr_title: Allow deletion of unhealthy pods if enough healthy
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind bug


**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Currently, if you have a PDB with 0 disruptions
available and you attempt to evict a non-healthy
pod, the eviction request will always fail.  This
is because the eviction API does not currently
take in to account that the pod you are removing
is the unhealthy one.

This commit accounts for trying to evict an
unhealthy pod as long as there are enough healthy
pods to satisfy the PDB's requirements.  To
protect against race conditions, a ResourceVersion
constraint is enforced.  This will ensure that
the target pod does not go healthy and allow
any race condition to occur which might disrupt
too many pods at once.

This commit also exports a public function
from the disruption controller to ensure we
always calculate pod health in the same manner
as PDBs.  This will help prevent regressions.


**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:

Fixes #80389

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:
yes

```release-note
Unhealthy pods covered by PDBs can be successfully evicted if enough healthy pods are available.
```

**Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.**:

```docs

```

@deads2k You helped review the previous eviction patch, would you mind taking a look at this one?

I think this is an improvement over the existing behavior where all running but non-ready pods would be blocked from eviction no matter the value in the PDB. I'm still a bit concerned that this doesn't fully resolve the discrepancy between what is considered a healthy/ready pod in the disruption controller and the eviction service. A pod that is running but not ready will still not be counted as available by the disruption controller, but is still blocked from eviction.

This makes me wonder if the outcome here is the same as if we changed the criteria in both the disruption controller and in the eviction service so that any pod that is in the running phase is considered `available` and therefore eviction of the pod must check for PDBs?

@mortent 
> I'm still a bit concerned that this doesn't fully resolve the discrepancy between what is considered a healthy/ready pod in the disruption controller and the eviction service. 

That's what this line is intended to address: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/94381/files#diff-af923020fb5800d949a2b1acd9117903R693

Exporting that function and then calling it from the eviction API ensures we're using the same logic to determine pod as healthy/disrupted.

> A pod that is running but not ready will still not be counted as available by the disruption controller, but is still blocked from eviction.

This is exactly what this patch set is intended to change.  Now, if a pod is not ready, it will be unblocked from eviction as long as there are enough *other* healthy pods.

> This makes me wonder if the outcome here is the same as if we changed the criteria in both the disruption controller and in the eviction service so that any pod that is in the running phase is considered `available` and therefore eviction of the pod must check for PDBs?

I'm not sure what you mean by this.  The current criteria is 'healthy' == 'Ready'.  If we made 'healthy' == 'Running' then that would undermine the effectiveness of PDBs.

For example, imagine you have data sharded across 3 pods.  pod 'A' goes down, the replacement pod 'A' comes up.  That pod is running, but not 'ready.'  It's not 'ready' because it's replicating the data from the other 2 hosts that are primary on itself.  If we treated pod 'A' as healthy and then evicted pod 'B', then we lose data.

> That's what this line is intended to address: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/94381/files#diff-af923020fb5800d949a2b1acd9117903R693
> 
> Exporting that function and then calling it from the eviction API ensures we're using the same logic to determine pod as healthy/disrupted.

I think that is fine. What I was thinking about is that a pod that is `running` but not `ready` will not be counted as available by the disruption controller, which would suggest it is not ready/healthy. But the eviction API will not evict a pod in the same state without checking against the PDB. So the pod is in some ways not healthy enough to be counted as available by the disruption controller, but at the same time we check against the very same PDB in order to allow eviction.

Even with this fix, it seems like situations as the one described in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/72320 can still happen. In the end, this comes down to the question of when it is safe to evict a pod that is in CrashLoopBackoff, which is discussed at length in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/80389 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83906.

> 
> I'm not sure what you mean by this. The current criteria is 'healthy' == 'Ready'. If we made 'healthy' == 'Running' then that would undermine the effectiveness of PDBs.

Yeah, you are right. I didn't think this through.

> 
> For example, imagine you have data sharded across 3 pods. pod 'A' goes down, the replacement pod 'A' comes up. That pod is running, but not 'ready.' It's not 'ready' because it's replicating the data from the other 2 hosts that are primary on itself. If we treated pod 'A' as healthy and then evicted pod 'B', then we lose data.

Not sure I follow this. There is certainly an availability issue, but seems unavoidable as long as containers are crashlooping. Presumably any data that needs to be persisted across pod failures is on a persistent volume and can be mounted into a replacement pod when it comes up.

Anyway, this PR already has lgtm, so we need an approver to take a look at this.
/assign @janetkuo @soltysh

@mortent 
> Even with this fix, it seems like situations as the one described in #72320 can still happen. In the end, this comes down to the question of when it is safe to evict a pod that is in CrashLoopBackoff, which is discussed at length in #80389 and #83906.

This patch would allow you to evict a single pod that is in crash loop backoff if there are enough other healthy pods covered by the PDB.  Blocking eviction when there are not enough healthy pods is pretty much the entire point of the eviction API, so if all pods are in crash loop backoff, I would expect eviction to always fail.  We can't automatically know if the crashloop backoff will happen indefinitely or if it's just a temporary condition (eg, on start, check some web service, if down, exit 1, repeat).

Generally speaking, PDBs are a single tool in a large tool set.  Administrators and/or application owners have some responsibility to ensure their nodes aren't crashloop-backoff wastelands if they want to use the eviction API.  This might include monitoring and alerting, or some other controller that is smart enough to do the right thing.  I most cases eviction API refers to someone draining a node, so it's trivial to look at the output of the drain command and just delete the broken pods.

> Presumably any data that needs to be persisted across pod failures is on a persistent volume and can be mounted into a replacement pod when it comes up.

I agree with this, unless the pod is something like a ceph OSD, and 'evicting' pod A is part of the process of deleting the node in which it's running on and it's underlying storage.  Anyway, in the general case, we can't assume what a pod is doing, and I think the current guidelines to count healthy==ready make sense.

> This patch would allow you to evict a single pod that is in crash loop backoff if there are enough other healthy pods covered by the PDB. Blocking eviction when there are not enough healthy pods is pretty much the entire point of the eviction API, so if all pods are in crash loop backoff, I would expect eviction to always fail. We can't automatically know if the crashloop backoff will happen indefinitely or if it's just a temporary condition (eg, on start, check some web service, if down, exit 1, repeat).

That is fair. But we can use ResourceVersion to make sure we don't evict pods that have become Ready, and controllers will usually replace any evicted pods. If a pod isn't owned by a controller, eviction will be problematic in all situations.

> Generally speaking, PDBs are a single tool in a large tool set. Administrators and/or application owners have some responsibility to ensure their nodes aren't crashloop-backoff wastelands if they want to use the eviction API. This might include monitoring and alerting, or some other controller that is smart enough to do the right thing. I most cases eviction API refers to someone draining a node, so it's trivial to look at the output of the drain command and just delete the broken pods.

This is true for running a small number of clusters. At scale, looking at the output of drain commands and manually delete pods quickly becomes impractical. I think the eviction API is used by cluster autoscalers where there aren't anyone who can manually look at this. It is also an important tool for doing node upgrades, which again will often be performed by automation and usually by a different team/company than the owners of the workloads.
Whenever possible, we should try to avoid situations that require manual intervention.

> That is fair. But we can use ResourceVersion to make sure we don't evict pods that have become Ready, and controllers will usually replace any evicted pods. If a pod isn't owned by a controller, eviction will be problematic in all situations.

My concern isn't necessarily draining the individual pod, but if there is an automated process that's going to drain several nodes at once, or as I mentioned, serially drain nodes resulting in multiple pods from a set being evicted.  If a pod isn't owned by a controller, the user can still elect to specify a PDB.  They might have some off-cluster component that is watching their pods and ensuring proper amount and deployment, or it might just be a development pod, etc.

> Whenever possible, we should try to avoid situations that require manual intervention.

I completely agree.  My primary use case for this is automated systems, especially cluster-api.  Projects/administrators have more tools at their disposal than just running drain with default options.  After a timeout, they could consider using https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/88337 to specify custom pod filters and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/85571 to force delete instead of eviction.  For example, after running normal drain for some length of time, they write a filter to exclude all pods that aren't in a state they wish to ignore (eg, crashloop backoff), and specify the disable-eviction option.  This will result in just crash-loop backoff pods being removed.

In any case, a node being blocked from drain by an automated system is no worse off in this scenario as currently, if there's a healthy pod you want to drain and disrupted pods elsewhere, you won't be able to.  Inevitably, there are going to be situations where administrators have to intervene or use brute-force and potentially disrupt applications.  We can't solve all those scenarios in the eviction API, IMO.
/approve

issue_context.title: PDBs using minUnavailable prevent draining unready pods
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->

**What happened**:

We were unable to drain pods on an unhealthy node that were stuck in pod initializing. The disruption budget has a `minAvailable` of 2. We had two healthy pods and a pod stuck in initializing thus it's unhealthy. A drain on the node with the unhealthy pod stuck in initializing was prevented. 

**What you expected to happen**:

The pods should have been evicted because they are in a not Ready state. 

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Using a PDB with `minAvailable` attempt to drain a node with a pod in a not Ready state. 

**Anything else we need to know?**:

The reason this is prevented is because the disruption controller determines the number of allowed disruptions by looking at [`currentHealthy - desiredHealthy`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a07b027261383127494fc6d4e3ca2c544fb4a464/pkg/controller/disruption/disruption.go#L749-L752). When `minAvailable` is used your `desiredHealthy` count becomes that value, which in our case is 2. The `currentHealthy` count is 2 also because the 3rd pod is stuck in an initializing state on the bad node. This leaves the PDB with an allowed disruption of 0 and thus blocks the drain. 

The eviction logic in the storage only allows pods in a terminal state to bypass the PDB. 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L124-L133

If they're not in a terminal state the eviction will only be allowed to occur if there are allowable disruptions available on the PDB.

It seems that the storage logic should allow draining pods that are not ready instead of just allowing terminal pods. 

/sig apps

I'm still interested in this.  I'm hoping the ignore-pending case will merge at some point, and then we can investigate this.

I think between how we're doing deletion of pending (enforcing deletionOptions that ensure pod has not changed revision) and my other patch that checks current PDB count (not include the broken pod) is stable could work.

Since 'NotReady' is possibly transitive, we would need to ensure we always verify PDBs before removing a pod in this state.  It might be 'NotReady' because it's replicating data from another pod, etc, and removing it without checking there are enough healthy replicas could cause data loss, IMO.

If it's not ready because it's replicating data from another pod then the data exists in the pod it is replicating from.

If a pod is not ready then it does not contribute to the satisfaction of the PodDisruptionBudget constraint and deleting it will not cause that constraint to be violated.

How about this scenario:

I have 3 pods.  1 pod hit some kind of problem, and the process exits.  The process takes some minutes to warm up, but all data is present.  This pod is 'NotReady' but otherwise working fine.  Simultaneously, another pod on a different node dies because the node crashes, never to return.

If we disregard PDBs in this scenario, we risk data loss by terminating the NotReady pod without regard to PDBs.

I think in this scenario, even if we check PDBs, we still might violate due to a race condition.

I'm not sure we can safely do this compared to the behavior we have today, at least not for the 'Not Ready' condition or any condition that indicates the pod is in 'Running' phase.  All we can say for certain when a pod is not ready is that it's not service traffic behind a to a service.  It could be do any number of things.

We might be able to tackle this on the drain client side with additional filters and options.  For instance, if a Pod is stuck in some non-Ready state, and has a lastTransitionTime > some configurable time, we could force delete that pod.

I would say the proposed fix is worse than the problem. It can take a long time for a database to replicate and a too-short timeout on forced deletion will lead to data loss.

A replication factor of two is vulnerable to two failures happening within the time it takes to replicate. That is fundamental.

I do believe you're conflating the ability of a pod to handle requests with ability for a database to handle loss of nodes. For our StatefulSets we have the data pods indicate readiness on ability to handle requests and then have a Deployment of pods that indicate readiness on the ability of the database to tolerate loss of data pods. The PodDisruptionBudget then includes both StatefulSet and Deployment in its selector.

So, I disagree.  Allowing it to be ignored (or force-deleted) client-side with a configurable timeout (say, 24hr last transition) results in the same thing as ignoring PDBs for this purpose:  the pod goes away.  Client-side fix is not worse than the problem, especially considering we can make the use opt-in (not default), and the timeout is configurable.  It's up to the user to decide when or if they wish to use that option.

Unfortunately, we can't assume anything about an application based on PDBs alone.  While some users might be utilizing pod readiness and PDBs in the manner you describe, probably not all are.

> For our StatefulSets we have the data pods indicate readiness on ability to handle requests 

In this scenario, a pod could have valid data that will be utilized for quorum once it rejoins, but is not yet ready.  It's not safe to ignore PDBs here if a pod is not ready, because we don't know if was previously ready, or just finished replicating all data from another (now gone) pod and is about to become ready, or what.  The pod could immediately transition to ready at any time and fix or keep an application from breaking.

Context, is of course, everything here.  The node in question was unhealthy (I presume unreachable is the more definitive state).  The eviction API doesn't consider what state the node is in.  The client doing the eviction can.

The context is also, IMO, automated systems trying to drain an unhealthy node.  We've already made the determination that the node is unhealthy and we want to remove workloads.  Most likely, that node is about to go away.  If it's just an admin running commands from the CLI, it's simple enough to delete a stuck pod and re-run drain.  An automated system can't really do this.

The tradeoff here is between never violating PDBs no matter what (current behavior of drain/eviction) or sometimes ignoring them.

@michaelgugino:
> I have 3 pods. 1 pod hit some kind of problem, and the process exits. The process takes some minutes to warm up, but all data is present. This pod is 'NotReady' but otherwise working fine. Simultaneously, another pod on a different node dies because the node crashes, never to return.
> 
> If we disregard PDBs in this scenario, we risk data loss by terminating the NotReady pod without regard to PDBs.

Does the current drain/eviction procedure code handle this scenario at all? Let's say I have a deployment with `replicas: 3` and a PDB with `minUnavailable: 2`. A node gets drained so one pod gets evicted, then before a new pod is fully started another pod crashes. This leaves just one available pod, violating the PDB.

> A node gets drained so one pod gets evicted, then before a new pod is fully started another pod crashes.

This would be an involuntary disruption, which PDBs can't defend against.  There are some other issues with PDBs that make this situation more complex as far as preserving the crashed node for any DR purposes, but there is always a window of time where data loss can occur.

> The tradeoff here is between never violating PDBs no matter what (current behavior of drain/eviction) or sometimes ignoring them.

If, as in the OP, there is a PDB with `minAvailable: 2` with two ready pods and one non-ready pod, how does evicting the non-ready pod cause the PDB to be violated? There are still two available pods.

If the pod were healthy it would have been evicted.

> > The tradeoff here is between never violating PDBs no matter what (current behavior of drain/eviction) or sometimes ignoring them.
> 
> If, as in the OP, there is a PDB with `minAvailable: 2` with two ready pods and one non-ready pod, how does evicting the non-ready pod cause the PDB to be violated? There are still two available pods.
> 
> If the pod were healthy it would have been evicted.

Yeah, as long as we're validating we have the minAvailable, I think we could be okay.  There are opportunities for race conditions, but those would be involuntary disruptions and aren't covered in the code as is anyway.
/reopen

Can you explain from history *why* we were returning TooManyRequests in this code base?  Was it a quick workaround to trigger retry?  Or was there a longer discussion about the appropriate response code.  I don't have confidence from the comments here that it's the right error code, and I'd want to be confident before we spread it to a second spot (and update the comments such that it's explicitly clear that no other status code is appropriate, if so)

Here's the original implementing PR, this comment makes me believe that we chose an error number out of a hat: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/31033#discussion_r75573684

Current state of the world as far as kubectl/drain is that while trying to evict a pod, if I get a 429, that indicates the PDB did not allow eviction at this time, retry.

We are sending 429 here to emulate a blocking PDB (eg, PDB with 0 disruptions available) as we do above.  This is because if we fail the ResourceVersion constraint here, we are no longer in position to evaluate the PDBs.

I think signaling the client to optionally retry is the most sensible option here, and fits the current behavior: If I had 0 disruptions left (because the pod I'm trying to evict is already disrupted) we send back a 429.

Thinking about the status codes we've assigned in the past (as the rough originator of most of the error stanzas I probably should create on separately for this if we will use it in the future), there's a couple that are close but not equivalent:

If you specify `generateName` and we keep getting collisions - the server generates a random name and then attempts to create the object in etcd, which could fail because someone else could choose that name - after 10 we return ServerTimeout

```
// NewServerTimeout returns an error indicating the requested action could not be completed due to a
// transient error, and the client should try again.
```

Patch retries forever, as does a guaranteed update.
I guess 429 is fine for now, I can't really think of a better one and I'd rather not couple this change to to a more dramatic client behavior change.
